title: Organs: what is inside the body, and how the parts work together
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers NIOS Class 5 Lesson 13 'Internal Organs of the Human Body' (skeleton, joints and muscles, digestive organs, lungs, heart and blood, kidneys, brain and nerves, reproductive organs). No textbook needed.
summary: Your heart has beaten hundreds of millions of times, and you never once told it to. Your child finds out what the skeleton protects: lungs that fill when a muscle underneath pulls down, a heart that pumps blood round in a circle, kidneys that filter all the blood many times a day, and a brain that controls it all through nerves. They build a bottle lung, listen to a heartbeat through a funnel, filter model blood and time their own reactions. Then they find out that organs work as a team, that the body has spare capacity, that a kidney can work inside another person, and that scientists still argue about what counts as an organ.
builds_on: Class 1: body parts, bones, joints and muscles. Class 4: the skeleton's four jobs, including protecting organs (skull, ribs, spine), muscle pairs, and other kinds of skeleton. Here: the organs themselves and the systems they form. The Class 5 lesson on digestion follows food through the gut in detail.
subconcepts: an organ is a body part with a special job, made of tissues and cells
organ systems: organs working as a team
voluntary and involuntary muscles, and the heart muscle that never rests
lungs, the diaphragm and the alveoli: getting oxygen in and carbon dioxide out
the heart, a four-chambered pump, and blood going round in a circle (circulation and the pulse)
kidneys filter the blood and make urine, and the bladder stores it
the brain, spinal cord and nerves: messages and reflexes
the digestive organs in one journey, and the liver's hundreds of jobs
homeostasis: feedback loops keep the body just right
nerves send fast messages, hormones send slow ones
where our organs came from: each one first appeared in older animals and was passed down
reproductive organs, with their correct names, and how every baby begins
spare capacity and organ donation: one kidney can be enough, and can live on in another person
how we came to know: from Ibn al-Nafis to Harvey
is the list of organs finished? new organs and old arguments
goals: By the end your child can place the brain, lungs, heart, liver, stomach, intestines, kidneys and bladder correctly on a body outline and say each one's job.
By the end your child can explain how breathing works using the diaphragm, and what the lungs swap.
By the end your child can explain that blood goes round in a circle pumped by the heart, and find and count their pulse.
By the end your child can explain what the kidneys do and why urine colour tells us about water.
By the end your child can tell voluntary from involuntary actions and explain a reflex.
By the end your child can name the reproductive organs correctly and say simply how a baby begins.
By the end your child can explain how organs depend on each other, and why a person can give a kidney and stay healthy.
words: organ
a body part made of different tissues that does a special job, like the heart or a kidney
organ system
a team of organs that work together, like the lungs, windpipe and diaphragm for breathing
diaphragm
the dome-shaped muscle under the lungs. When it pulls down, air flows in.
alveoli
millions of tiny air bags in the lungs where oxygen passes into the blood
artery
a tube that carries blood away from the heart
vein
a tube that carries blood back to the heart
pulse
the beat you can feel in an artery each time the heart pumps
kidney
a bean-shaped organ that filters waste and extra water out of the blood
urine
the waste water made by the kidneys, stored in the bladder
nerve
a thread of cells that carries messages between the brain and the body
reflex
a fast action the body does without thinking, like pulling your hand from something hot
involuntary
happening without you choosing, like your heartbeat

days.title: What is inside the cage?
days.goal: Recall the skeleton's job of protecting, and start a life-size map of the organs.

steps.title: Remember the cage
steps.do: Ask your child: 'In Class 4 you learnt four jobs of the skeleton. Which one is about protecting?' (the skull covers the brain, the ribs cover the heart and lungs, the spine covers the spinal cord). 'What do you think is so important that it needs a cage of bone?' Write their guesses down. Then ask them to name a pair of muscles that work together (biceps and triceps).

steps.title: What is an organ?
steps.do: Say: 'Your body is made of trillions of tiny living cells. Cells of the same kind join to make a tissue, like muscle or nerve. Different tissues join to make an organ, a body part with a special job. Organs that work together make an organ system.' Show it with blocks: one block is a cell, a row is a tissue, a small tower is an organ and a whole building is a system. Ask: 'Is your skin an organ?' (yes, the biggest one: it has several tissues and several jobs). 'Is a bone an organ?' (yes, each bone counts as an organ too).

steps.title: Life-size organ map
steps.do: Start Activity a1 and the project. Draw round your child on a big sheet. Cut organ shapes from coloured paper, using the sizes in the activity: a brain, two lungs, a heart, a liver, a stomach, a long strip of small intestine, a fat strip of large intestine, two kidneys and a bladder. Your child places them where they think they go. Do not glue yet: you will move them as you learn. Ask: 'Which surprised you most?' (often that the heart is near the middle, and that the liver is so big).

steps.title: Your hand is a ruler
steps.do: Show your child that their fist is about the size of their own heart. Put the fist in the middle of the chest, tipped slightly to the left: 'That is where your heart is.' Put both fists on the back, just above the waist, one on each side of the spine: 'Your kidneys are here, tucked under the bottom ribs. Each one is a little smaller than your fist.'

need: a big sheet of paper or newspaper taped together
a few blocks or small boxes (optional)

days.title: Lungs and breathing
days.goal: Model how breathing works and find out what the lungs swap.

steps.title: Breath count
steps.do: Your child sits still for one minute while you count their breaths (one in and one out is one breath). Then they hop on the spot for one minute and you count again. Write both numbers. Ask: 'Why do you think it went up?' (working muscles need more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide). Then: 'Put your hands on your lower ribs and breathe in deeply. What moves?' (the ribs lift out and the tummy pushes out).

steps.title: The bottle lung
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. A grown-up makes the model first: a plastic bottle with its bottom cut off, a balloon inside as a lung, and a balloon sheet stretched across the bottom as the diaphragm. Ask: 'What will happen to the balloon inside if you pull the bottom sheet down?' Your child pulls it down: the balloon fills. They push it up: the balloon empties. Ask: 'What is the bottom sheet standing for?' (the diaphragm). 'Did we blow air into the balloon?' (no, air flowed in by itself because the space inside the bottle got bigger).

steps.title: Into the blood
steps.do: Say: 'Air goes in at the nose and down the windpipe. The windpipe splits into two tubes, one for each lung, and these branch again and again into smaller tubes. At the very ends are about 500 million tiny air bags called alveoli. Each one is wrapped in tiny blood tubes. Oxygen passes through their thin walls into the blood. Carbon dioxide, a waste gas from your cells, passes the other way, and you breathe it out.' Ask: 'If you spread all the alveoli out flat, how big do you think they would be?' (nearly the size of a badminton court, which is why so much oxygen can get in).

steps.title: Smoke and dust
steps.do: Ask: 'What do you think happens to the smoke and dust we breathe in?' Then explain: the tubes are lined with sticky mucus and tiny hairs that sweep dirt up and out, which is why we cough. But smoke from cigarettes and beedis, burning rubbish and the smoggy winter air in many Indian cities damages the alveoli. Ask: 'Who in our town breathes the most smoke?' (people who work near traffic, families who cook on wood fires without a chimney). 'What could change that?' Listen, and let your child give their own ideas.

need: a 1-litre plastic bottle, scissors (grown-up cuts), two balloons, a rubber band, tape, modelling clay

days.title: The heart and the great circle
days.goal: Hear the heart, count the pulse and understand that blood goes round in a circle.

steps.title: Funnel stethoscope and pulse
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Push a kitchen funnel into a length of plastic tube. Your child holds the open end of the tube gently near their ear while you hold the funnel on their chest, a little left of the middle. Listen for 'lub-dub'. Then find the pulse on the inside of the wrist with two fingers, not the thumb. Count for 30 seconds and double it. Count again after one minute of skipping.

steps.title: A pump with four rooms
steps.do: Draw a heart as a box with four rooms, called chambers: two small ones on top (the atria) and two big ones below (the ventricles). A wall separates the left side from the right side. Explain: 'The right side pumps blood that has used up its oxygen to the lungs. There it picks up fresh oxygen and comes back to the left side. The left side pumps it all round the body. So blood goes through the heart twice on every round trip.' Ask: 'The wall of the left side is thicker. Why do you think that is?' (it has to push blood all the way to the toes and the brain). Say: 'The lub-dub you heard is the sound of valves, small flaps like doors, snapping shut so blood cannot flow backwards.'

steps.title: Who found the circle?
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v1: Ibn al-Nafis and William Harvey. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1 on organs, lungs and heart. For each written question, ask your child to explain it aloud first.

need: a kitchen funnel, about 50 cm of plastic tubing, a clock with seconds

days.title: Kidneys: the body's filters
days.goal: Model how kidneys clean blood and read the body's water signal.

steps.title: How much water?
steps.do: Ask: 'How much liquid do you think your two kidneys filter out of your blood in one day?' Let them guess. Then say: 'About 180 litres, nearly a big drum full. They put back almost all of it, and send only one or two litres out as urine.' Ask: 'Why not throw it all away?' (you would dry out).

steps.title: A model kidney
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. Make model blood: water with a few drops of food colouring (the waste), a handful of dried peas or rajma (the blood cells) and some rice (the proteins). Ask: 'What will go through the sieve, and what will stay behind?' Pour it through a sieve lined with a thin cloth over a jar. Look at what went through. Explain that each kidney has about a million tiny filters. Then the kidney takes back the water and the useful things the body needs, which our sieve cannot do.

steps.title: Read the story
steps.do: Read aloud 'Half of Enough', the story in this lesson. It is told by a kidney. Before reading, say: 'This story is told by a kidney. Nobody dies in it.' After reading, ask the story questions.

steps.title: The first kidney gift
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v3: the first successful kidney transplant, between twin brothers in 1954. Ask: 'Why do you think the first one was between identical twins?' (their bodies are so alike that one body does not attack the other's kidney as a stranger). Then ask the voice question.

need: water, food colouring, dried peas or rajma, rice, a sieve, a thin cotton cloth such as an old handkerchief, two jars

days.title: The brain and the messengers
days.goal: Find out how the brain and nerves control the body, and time a reflex.

steps.title: Did you choose that?
steps.do: Ask your child to do each of these and say 'I chose it' or 'I didn't choose it': wave, blink (after keeping the eyes open a long time), swallow, heartbeat, breathe, scratch the nose, sneeze. Say: 'Muscles you control are called voluntary, like your arm muscles. Muscles that work by themselves are involuntary, like your heart and stomach. Breathing is both: it goes on by itself, but you can hold your breath for a while.'

steps.title: The ruler drop
steps.do: Do Experiment e4. Hold a 30 cm ruler at the top. Your child holds finger and thumb open at the zero end, without touching it. Drop it without warning, and they catch it as fast as they can. Read the centimetre mark where they caught it. Try five times with each hand, then three times while they count backwards from 50. Ask first: 'Will counting backwards make you faster or slower? Why?' Afterwards ask what happened (most children are slower, because the brain is busy with another job).

steps.title: Brain, cord and nerves
steps.do: Say: 'Your brain weighs about 1.3 kilograms. It is soft, and it floats in liquid inside the skull. It has about 86 billion nerve cells. Nerves run from it, down the spinal cord inside your backbone, to every part of you. They carry messages as tiny electrical signals.' Draw the brain and show three parts: the big wrinkled cerebrum (thinking, seeing, feeling, choosing), the cerebellum at the back (balance and smooth movement), and the brain stem, which joins the spinal cord (breathing and heartbeat). Then try a reflex. Your child sits with legs crossed, and you tap gently just below the kneecap with the side of your hand. The leg kicks. Say: 'That message went to the spinal cord and straight back, without waiting for the brain. A reflex is a fast action you do not choose. It keeps you safe: you pull your hand off a hot tawa almost before you feel the pain.'

steps.title: Heart or brain?
steps.do: Tell your child: Aristotle, a great thinker in ancient Greece, believed that the heart was where we think and feel, and that the brain only cooled the blood. Ask: 'Why might he have thought so?' (the heart races when we are scared or excited, it is warm, and the brain looks like grey jelly). 'What evidence shows that we think with the brain?' (head injuries change thinking, and people with machine hearts think perfectly well). Ask: 'Why do we still say "I love you with all my heart"?'

days.title: Organs as a team
days.goal: Follow one meal and one breath through all the systems and see how every organ needs the others.

steps.title: Organ map check
steps.do: Go back to the organ map. Your child moves every organ to where it really belongs, then glues them down. Ask: 'Which organs have we met? Which have we not?' (the food organs and the liver).

steps.title: The food organs in one journey
steps.do: Trace a mouthful of food with a finger on the map: mouth, food pipe (oesophagus), stomach, small intestine (about 6 metres long in a grown-up, coiled up), large intestine, and out. Point to the liver: 'This is the biggest organ inside you. It makes bile, which breaks fat into small drops. It stores sugar and removes poisons from the blood. It has hundreds of jobs.' Tell your child about voice v4, Gerty Cori, who found how the liver and the muscles pass sugar back and forth, and ask her question. Say: 'Another lesson, on digestion, follows food in much more detail.'

steps.title: The Red Cell Run
steps.do: Play the board game g1. Each player is a red blood cell carrying oxygen round the body, and the squares are parts of the body. Talk about each square as you land on it.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2, which asks how organs depend on each other. Encourage full sentences with 'because'.

need: the printed board game, a die and counters

days.title: Keeping just right, and where our organs came from
days.goal: See how the body keeps itself balanced with fast nerve messages and slow hormone messages, and find out where our organs first came from.

steps.title: A bell and a drop
steps.do: Clap in one room while your child stands in the next room: they hear it at once. Then put one drop of food colouring into a still glass of water and watch it spread slowly for a minute. Say: 'Your body sends messages in two ways. Nerves are like the clap: fast electrical signals, for right now. Hormones are like the colour: chemicals let out into the blood. They spread everywhere slowly, and their effect lasts longer.'

steps.title: The slow messengers
steps.do: Name four hormones and where they come from. Adrenaline comes from the adrenal glands, which sit like small caps on top of the kidneys. When a dog barks suddenly, adrenaline makes the heart race and the breathing speed up, ready to run. Insulin comes from the pancreas, behind the stomach. After a meal it tells cells to take sugar out of the blood. Growth hormone comes from the pituitary, a gland the size of a pea under the brain. Much of it is let out during deep sleep. Melatonin comes from a tiny gland in the brain. It rises in the dark and helps us feel sleepy. Ask: 'Which hormone could explain why children grow while they sleep?' and 'Why might a bright screen at bedtime make it hard to fall asleep?'

steps.title: Drama: the Body Council
steps.do: Your child is the Brain, sitting on a chair. You and some toys are the helpers: Skin Sensor, Sweat Team, Heart Drummer and Adrenal Gland. Act out four situations, one at a time: a hot kitchen in May, a dog that barks suddenly, skipping lunch, and bedtime. For each one, the sensor reports ('Cheeks hot!'), the Brain decides, the team acts ('Sweat on!'), and the sensor reports again ('Cooler now'), so the Brain can switch it off. Say: 'Notice, act, check, stop: this is called a feedback loop. Your body keeps itself at about 37 degrees, with just enough water and sugar, by running loops like this all day. Keeping the body steady like this is called homeostasis.' End with bee breath (bhramari): hum softly on five slow breaths out. Say: 'Long, slow breaths out help your heart beat a little slower.'

steps.title: Where our organs came from
steps.do: Draw a long strip of paper as a timeline. From left to right, mark each of these with a small drawing. The first cells, with a thin oily covering, about 3.5 to 4 billion years ago (scientists think). Bacteria that went to live inside another cell and became mitochondria, the tiny parts that release energy in nearly every one of your cells, roughly 2 billion years ago. The first animals with nerves and muscles, more than 550 million years ago. The first backbones, in small fish-like swimmers, over 500 million years ago. Lungs, which first grew in fish over 400 million years ago, before any animal walked on land. Four limbs, about 370 million years ago. And you, today. Say: 'The covering of your cells, your nerves, your lungs and your backbone first appeared in other animals long ago, and were passed down to you.' Ask: 'Which of these surprised you most?'

need: a glass of water and food colouring
a long strip of paper and pencils

days.title: How every body begins, and is the list finished?
days.goal: Learn the reproductive organs by their correct names and weigh a live debate about new organs.

steps.title: A note for the parent, then the talk
steps.do: Parent note: children who know the correct names for their private parts are safer and less embarrassed, and doctors advise using them. Keep your voice calm and matter-of-fact, the same as for the heart. Say: 'Every person has reproductive organs. They are for making babies when a person is grown up. A girl has two ovaries inside her belly, which hold tiny eggs. She has a uterus, also called the womb, where a baby can grow. The opening outside is the vulva, and the passage inside is the vagina. A boy has two testes in a bag of skin called the scrotum. When he is grown, they will make sperm. He also has a penis. When a grown-up woman's egg and a grown-up man's sperm join, the joined cell can grow in the uterus for about nine months into a baby. You began as one cell, smaller than a full stop.' Answer questions simply and truthfully. It is fine to say 'That is a good question for when you are older' about anything you do not want to go into today.

steps.title: My body, my rules
steps.do: Agree your family's body-safety rules together and write them on the organ map. The parts covered by a swimsuit are private. Nobody should touch them or ask to see them, except a parent or doctor helping to keep you clean or healthy, and then a trusted grown-up is there. No secrets about touching, ever. You can always tell a trusted grown-up, and you will never be in trouble for telling. Name three trusted grown-ups.

steps.title: Is the list of organs finished?
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v2: the claim in 2018 that a network of spaces filled with fluid, all through the body, is an organ that had not been noticed. It is called the interstitium. Also tell them that in 2016 an Irish surgeon, J. Calvin Coffey, argued that the mesentery, the folded sheet that holds the intestines in place, should count as one organ. Ask: 'Who decides what counts as an organ? What would you need to see?'

steps.title: Spare parts
steps.do: Ask: 'How many kidneys does Revathi have at the end of the story?' (one). 'Is she ill?' (no). Explain: 'Most organs can do much more work than we usually need. One kidney can do the work of two, and it grows a little bigger. A person can live with one lung, or after losing a large part of the liver, which grows back.' Ask: 'Why might a body be built with spare capacity?' (for emergencies, for hard work, and for getting older). Then ask: 'Is spare capacity wasted, or is it wise?'

days.title: Teach it back
days.goal: Review all the organs, do the challenge worksheet and teach it all back.

steps.title: Organ map tour
steps.do: Your child gives a tour of the finished organ map, pointing to each organ and saying its job in one sentence. Ask them to draw arrows showing one breath of oxygen going from the nose to a toe muscle (nose, windpipe, lungs, alveoli, blood, heart, artery, toe).

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3. These questions are hard. Let your child think aloud and argue with you.

steps.title: Big questions
steps.do: Ask: 'Your heart has beaten about 300 million times since you were born, and you never once told it to. Who is in charge of your body: you, or your body?'

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child teaches a grown-up how breathing, the heart and the kidneys work, using their models, and explains one reflex. Then ask the check questions.

sections.p: Match the organ to its job.
pairs: take in oxygen, give out carbon dioxide
filter waste out of the blood

the blood, pumped by the heart

sections.p: Voluntary or involuntary?
A reflex is fast because the message…

Blood goes through the heart how many times on one round trip of the body?

sections.p: The first kidney transplant that worked was between identical twins. Why?

Settled or still argued about?

how many organs the body has

Your body has spare capacity: two kidneys when one is enough. Is that wasteful or wise? Name something else in life that is better with a spare.

experiments.title: The bottle lung
experiments.question: How does the diaphragm make us breathe?
steps: A grown-up cuts the bottom off the bottle.
Push one balloon into the neck of the bottle so that it hangs inside, and stretch its mouth over the bottle neck. Seal the neck with clay so air can go in and out only through the balloon.
Cut the neck off the second balloon and stretch the rest over the open bottom of the bottle. Hold with a rubber band and tape.
Pinch the bottom sheet and pull it down gently. Watch the inside balloon.
Push the sheet up. Watch again.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'When you pull the bottom sheet down, will the balloon inside fill up or empty?'
experiments.observe: Pulling the sheet down makes the balloon inside fill up. Pushing it up makes the balloon shrink. If nothing happens, air is leaking: press the clay and tape tighter.
experiments.why: The bottom sheet is the diaphragm. When the diaphragm contracts, it pulls down, and rib muscles lift the ribs out, so the space in the chest gets bigger. The air pressure inside the lungs drops, and air from outside flows in. When the diaphragm relaxes, the space gets smaller and air is pushed out. We do not suck air in. The air outside pushes in to fill the space.
experiments.safety: Only a grown-up cuts the bottle. The cut edge can be sharp, so cover it with tape.

experiments.title: Funnel stethoscope and pulse count
experiments.question: How fast does the heart beat, and does it change?
need: about 50 cm of plastic tube that fits the funnel
a clock or phone with seconds
steps: Push the tube onto the funnel spout.
Your child holds the tube end gently near (not inside) their ear.
Hold the funnel flat on their chest, a little to the left of the middle, in a quiet room.
Listen for the 'lub-dub'.
Find the pulse on the thumb side of the inside of the wrist with two fingers. Count the beats for 30 seconds and double it.
Skip or jog on the spot for one minute and count again. Count again after two minutes of rest.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'How many beats in a minute? Will it go up or down after skipping?'
experiments.observe: A resting pulse for children of this age is often between 70 and 110 beats a minute. It goes up after exercise and comes down again with rest.
experiments.why: Each beat is the heart squeezing blood into the arteries. The arteries stretch with each push, and that is the pulse. When muscles work hard they need more oxygen and food, so the brain tells the heart to beat faster. The 'lub-dub' is the sound of the heart's valves closing to stop blood flowing backwards.
experiments.safety: Never put the tube inside the ear, and never shout into it.

experiments.title: A model kidney
experiments.question: How can a filter separate waste from useful things?
need: a handful of dried peas or rajma
a thin cotton cloth, such as an old handkerchief
steps: Make the 'blood': water with a few drops of food colouring (dissolved waste), peas (blood cells) and rice (big proteins).
Line the sieve with the cloth and hold it over a clear jar.
Pour the 'blood' through slowly.
Look at what went through and what stayed behind.
Talk about what is missing from the model.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which parts of the blood will go through the filter?'
experiments.observe: The coloured water goes through. The peas and rice stay behind.
experiments.why: Each kidney has about a million tiny filtering units called nephrons. Blood is pushed through very small filters. Water, salts, sugar and wastes such as urea get through, but blood cells and big proteins stay in the blood. Then the tubes of each nephron take back almost all the water, sugar and salt the body needs. What is left is waste in a little water: urine. Our model shows the first step but not the taking-back step.
experiments.safety: Do not drink the coloured water. Food colouring can stain clothes.

experiments.title: The ruler drop
experiments.question: How fast do messages travel from eyes to brain to hand?
steps: Hold the ruler at the 30 cm end so it hangs down.
Your child holds finger and thumb open around the 0 cm end, not touching.
Drop it without warning. Your child catches it.
Read the number at the top of their finger and write it down.
Do five tries with each hand, then three tries while they count backwards from 50 out loud.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which hand will be faster? Will counting backwards change it?'
experiments.observe: Catches are often between 10 and 25 cm. A catch at about 15 cm means the child took about one-sixth of a second to react. Counting backwards usually makes the catch lower down the ruler, which means slower.
experiments.why: The eyes see the ruler fall. A message goes along nerves to the brain. The brain decides and sends a message along nerves to the finger muscles. Each step takes time. When the brain is busy with another job, deciding takes longer. A reflex, like the knee jerk, is faster because the message does not go through the brain.
experiments.safety: Safe. Hold the ruler only a little above your child's hand, so it does not hit anyone as it falls.

activities.title: Life-size organ map
steps: Draw round your child lying on the paper.

Cut organs to these rough sizes for your child's body: brain (two fists), each lung (a cone about one and a half hands long), heart (one fist), liver (a wide wedge as big as two hands, under the right ribs), stomach (a J shape the size of a hand, on the left), small intestine (a strip about three times your child's height, coiled), large intestine (a fat strip around the coils), two kidneys (bean shapes a little smaller than a fist) and a bladder (a small balloon shape low in the middle).
Place them where your child thinks they go.
On Day 6, move them to the right places and glue them down.
Add the body-safety rules on Day 7.
activities.outcome: A life-size map of your child's own organs, used and corrected through the week.

project.title: The organ map and the team chart
steps: Make the life-size organ map (Activity a1).
Draw lines between organs that depend on each other, and write why on each line, for example 'the lungs give oxygen to the blood'.
Draw the path of one breath of oxygen in red, and the path of some waste in yellow (blood to kidneys to bladder).
Write the body-safety rules in a corner.
On the last day, use it to teach someone what you learnt.
project.outcome: A life-size organ map with team lines showing how organs depend on each other.

game.title: The Red Cell Run
rules: You are a red blood cell. Start in the LUNGS and pick up 3 oxygen tokens.
Roll and move along the path, which goes round in a loop.
Each time you land on a body square, drop off one oxygen token there and say why that part of the body needs oxygen.
When you run out of oxygen, go straight back to the LUNGS square on your next turn to fill up.
The first player to deliver 10 oxygen tokens wins.
squares: BRAIN: drop 1 oxygen. The brain uses about one-fifth of all the oxygen you breathe in
Skipping rope! Muscles need more: drop 2
Valve slams shut: no going back
KIDNEY: get filtered, miss a turn
Cold day: blood is kept away from the skin, go back 1
Right ventricle: push to the lungs, +2
Heart muscle itself needs feeding: drop 1

big: Your nerves, lungs and backbone first appeared in other animals long ago. What does that tell you about how you are related to them?
Your heart has beaten about 300 million times and you never told it to. Who is in charge of your body?
A kidney from one sister can live and work inside the other. Is that kidney now part of the second sister?
Is it fair that some people wait years for an organ and others never need one? Who should decide who gets one first?
Scientists still argue about what counts as an organ. Can a list of body parts ever be finished?
Is a body with spare parts wasteful or wise?

challenge.q: People say your heart is on the left side of your chest. Is that right?
challenge.hint: Your heart sits almost in the middle, behind the breastbone. It is tipped so that its lower end points to the left, which is why the beat feels strongest on the left. In about 1 person in 10,000 the heart is on the right instead, and they are usually perfectly healthy. Ask: why do you think people believe the heart is far on the left?

challenge.q: People say we think and love with our hearts. Is that right?
challenge.hint: Aristotle thought the heart did the thinking. The evidence now clearly shows that the brain does. Injuries to the brain change thinking and feeling, and people with machine heart pumps think and love as before. But the heart does respond to feelings. It races when we are scared or excited, because the brain sends it messages. Ask: why do you think so many languages kept the heart for love?

challenge.q: People say we use only 10 per cent of our brain. Is that true?
challenge.hint: This is a myth. Brain scans show that over a day almost every part of the brain is active, and damage to any part causes problems. The brain uses about a fifth of the body's oxygen, and a body would not spend that on parts it did not use. Ask: why might a myth like this spread?

challenge.q: People say organs are like machine parts that can be swapped like a car's. Is that true?
challenge.hint: A transplanted organ can work very well. But the new body's defences see it as a stranger and try to attack it, so most people with a transplant take medicines every day for life. Ask: how is a body different from a machine?

perspectives.who: A dialysis nurse in a hospital in Chennai
perspectives.view: She looks after people whose kidneys have stopped working. A machine cleans their blood for about four hours, three times a week. Ask: what would you miss most if you had to spend twelve hours a week attached to a machine?

perspectives.who: A family who agreed to donate their son's organs after he died in an accident
perspectives.view: In India, the family of a person who has died can choose to give that person's organs, and one donor can save several lives. Many families say it gave meaning to their loss. Ask: why might a family find it hard to decide, and why might it help them?

perspectives.who: An ancient Indian vaidya following the Charaka Samhita
perspectives.view: Ayurveda describes the body through doshas, dhatus (tissues) and channels called srotas. This is a different map from modern anatomy. Some of its advice about digestion and daily habits matches modern ideas, but its picture of how organs work does not. Ask: can two different maps of the same body both teach us something?

voices.who: Ibn al-Nafis (about 1213–1288), Damascus and Cairo, and William Harvey (1578–1657), England
voices.idea: For over a thousand years, doctors followed Galen, a Greek doctor in Rome. He taught that blood seeped through tiny holes in the wall of the heart, and that it was made fresh in the liver and used up. In about 1242 Ibn al-Nafis, an Arab doctor, wrote that there are no such holes. Blood must go from the right side of the heart through the lungs, mix with air there, and come back to the left side. In 1628 William Harvey showed by careful measuring that the heart pumps far more blood in an hour than the body could make. So the same blood must go round and round. This is called circulation.
voices.then: Ibn al-Nafis's work was hardly known in Europe. Some doctors mocked Harvey and called him a crank, and he lost patients. But within his lifetime many doctors accepted his idea.
voices.now: Both were right. Ibn al-Nafis's description was found again only in 1924, by the Egyptian doctor Muhyo Al-Deen Altawi, who read an old manuscript in Berlin. Many textbooks still give Harvey all the credit.
voices.ask: Ibn al-Nafis worked out the lung circuit 400 years before Harvey, but nearly nobody in Europe read his book. Is a discovery that nobody hears about still a discovery? Who should get the credit?

voices.who: Petros Benias, Neil Theise and colleagues (New York, published 2018), and their critics
voices.idea: Using a new kind of microscope inside living patients, the team saw a network of spaces filled with fluid and held up by fibres, in layers all through the body: under the skin, and around the gut, lungs and blood vessels. They argued that this 'interstitium' should be counted as an organ, perhaps one of the biggest in the body.
voices.then: Newspapers called it a 'new organ'. Many anatomists objected that the spaces were already known and that calling them an organ was a change of name, not a discovery.
voices.now: Scientists still disagree. Everyone agrees that these spaces and their fluid exist. The argument is about whether they make one organ. A similar argument happened in 2016, when the surgeon J. Calvin Coffey argued that the mesentery should be counted as one organ.
voices.ask: If two people agree on what they see but disagree on what to call it, is that a science argument or a word argument? Does it matter?

voices.who: Gerty Cori (1896–1957), born in Prague, worked in the USA
voices.idea: With her husband Carl Cori, Gerty Cori found how the body stores and uses sugar. Working muscles break down their stored sugar, called glycogen, and make a substance called lactate. The blood carries the lactate to the liver, which turns it back into sugar (glucose) and sends it back to the muscles. This loop is called the Cori cycle: the body reuses its fuel.
voices.then: Universities kept offering Carl a job and Gerty none, or only a junior one at a small part of his pay. For years at Washington University in St Louis she was a 'research associate', paid far less, though they worked side by side as equals.
voices.now: The Cori cycle is in biology textbooks everywhere. In 1947 Gerty and Carl Cori shared the Nobel Prize with Bernardo Houssay, and she became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. She was made a full professor only that same year.
voices.ask: Gerty and Carl did the same work. Why do you think she was paid so much less? How could you check, today, whether two people doing the same work are treated fairly?

voices.who: Joseph Murray (1919–2012) and the brothers Ronald and Richard Herrick, Boston, USA, 1954
voices.idea: Richard Herrick was dying because his kidneys had failed. His identical twin Ronald offered one of his own kidneys. On 23 December 1954, Joseph Murray's team moved Ronald's healthy kidney into Richard. It was the first organ transplant that kept working for a long time, because a twin's body does not attack the organ as a stranger.
voices.then: Some doctors thought it was wrong to operate on a healthy person who gained nothing for himself. Ronald decided anyway.
voices.now: Richard lived another eight years and married one of his nurses. Ronald lived until 2010 with one kidney. Medicines now let organs be given between people who are not twins, and kidney transplants save many thousands of lives every year, including in India. Murray shared the Nobel Prize in 1990. The donor's courage is less often remembered.
voices.ask: The doctor got the Nobel Prize. What did Ronald give? How should we remember people like him?

books.title: The Way We Work
books.author: David Macaulay
books.why: Detailed, funny cut-away drawings of every system in the body. Choose the breathing, heart and kidney pages to look at together.

books.title: The Magic School Bus Inside the Human Body
books.author: Joanna Cole
books.why: Ms Frizzle's class shrinks and rides through the stomach, blood, heart and brain: an adventure that maps the organs.

books.title: The Body: A Guide for Occupants
books.author: Bill Bryson
books.why: Full of astonishing true facts and stories of the people who found them, including some who were forgotten.

books.title: Me and My Amazing Body
books.author: Joan Sweeney
books.why: A simple first tour of the skeleton, muscles, heart, lungs and brain, told by a child.

check.q: What is an organ? Give three examples.
check.a: A body part made of tissues that does a special job, such as the heart, lungs, brain, kidneys, liver, stomach or skin.

check.q: How does the diaphragm make air come in?
check.a: It pulls down, making the chest space bigger, so air from outside rushes into the lungs.

check.q: Describe blood's journey through the heart.
check.a: The right side pumps blood to the lungs to get oxygen. The blood comes back to the left side, which pumps it round the body. Then it comes back to the right side. It goes round in a circle.
They filter waste and extra water out of the blood, keep what the body needs, and make urine, which is stored in the bladder.

check.q: What is a reflex? Give an example.
check.a: A fast action without thinking, where the message goes to the spinal cord and back, like the knee jerk or pulling a hand off something hot.

check.q: What are the reproductive organs for, and how does a baby begin?
check.a: For making babies when grown up. A baby begins when an egg from a woman's ovary and a sperm from a man's testes join, and it grows in the uterus for about nine months.

check.q: How can someone give a kidney and stay healthy?
check.a: One kidney can do the work of two, and it grows a little bigger. The body has spare capacity.

story.title: Half of Enough
text: I am a kidney. I am the shape of a rajma bean and the size of a fist, dark red and smooth, and for thirty-four years I lived on the right side of a woman called Revathi, tucked in under her bottom ribs, close to her back.

You will not have thought about me much. Nobody does. I am not like the heart, who gets songs written about her, or the brain, who thinks she runs the place. I work in the dark and I do not make a sound. But here is what I do: every few minutes, all of Revathi's blood passes through me and my twin on the left side. We let the water and the salts and the wastes slip through a million tiny sieves, and then, very carefully, we take back what she needs: the water, the sugar, the salt. What is left over, the waste in a little water, trickles down a long thin tube to the bladder. In a day, my twin and I sift through enough liquid to fill a drum. We keep almost all of it. We send away only what would harm her.

We are a pair, my twin and I. For thirty-four years we shared the work, and I will tell you a secret that only kidneys know. Either one of us could have done it alone. We were each half of enough. We were never more than half-busy.

Revathi has a younger sister, Sudha. They grew up in a two-room house in Madurai, sharing a bed, a tiffin, and every secret. When Sudha was twenty-eight, her kidneys began to fail. Nobody quite knew why. They got smaller and slower, and the wastes began to build up in her blood, and she grew tired and puffy and pale, and her skin itched, and food tasted of metal.

Three times a week, Sudha went to a hospital and sat for four hours with a tube in her arm while a machine cleaned her blood. It did a little of what her kidneys used to do. Only a little. On the other days she was too tired to play with her small son, Kannan, who did not understand why his mother slept so much.

I heard all this from inside Revathi. When she was worried, her heart beat faster, and the blood rushed through me quicker, and I could feel the change. On hot days, when she sweated a lot, I kept back more water for her, and her urine grew darker. I know Revathi's body better than she does.
One evening Revathi said to the doctor, “Take one of mine.”

There were many tests after that. Doctors took Revathi's blood and Sudha's blood and looked at them side by side. They were checking whether Sudha's body would be gentle with a stranger. Bodies are fierce about strangers. They have armies of white cells that hunt down anything that is not themselves. The doctors found that Revathi's blood and Sudha's were close enough, as sisters often are, and that with the right medicines every day, Sudha's armies could be calmed.
And then they chose me. The right one. I do not know why. Perhaps it was the shape of my blood tubes.

I will not tell you about the operation, because I was asleep, in a way, kept cold in an icy liquid in a steel dish. I remember Revathi's warmth, and then the cold, and then a long stillness. It was the first time in thirty-four years that no blood had passed through me.

But it was different. The doctors had not put me where I used to live, high and close to the back. They had put me low down, at the front, near Sudha's hip, and they had joined me to a big artery and a big vein there, and stitched my thin tube into her bladder. And then they let the blood in.

Oh, the blood. It came rushing in, red and fast, and it was full of waste: so much waste, months and months of it that no kidney had cleared. And it was Sudha's blood. It had a different taste. Her heart beat in a different rhythm, a little quicker than Revathi's, and her blood had different moods in it.

I did not stop to think. I did what kidneys do. I let the water and the salts and the wastes slip through my million sieves, and I took back what she needed, and I sent the rest away down the tube. The doctors were watching the tube. Before they had even finished sewing, there was urine in it.
Somebody in the operating room laughed out loud.
It has been a year now. I am doing the work of two, here near Sudha's hip, and I find I can. I was always able to. I was only ever half-busy before.

In the next room of my old home, Revathi's left kidney, my twin, is doing the work of two as well. My twin has grown a little bigger to manage. Revathi says she feels exactly the same as she ever did.

Last week Kannan climbed onto Sudha's lap, right on top of the place where I live, and asked her to come to the park. She went. I felt her heart speed up as she ran, and her blood rushing through me faster, and I worked faster, and I thought: so this is what all that spare was for.
story.epiphany: Organs do their jobs as a team: the heart pushes blood through the kidney, the kidney cleans it, and the bladder stores the urine. And the body is built with spare capacity: one kidney can do the work of two. The turn is the kidney's secret ('we were each half of enough') and the moment urine appears in the tube in Sudha's body. Underneath: one person's organ can work in another person, because human bodies share one plan, and the gift was a quiet one.
ask: What does a kidney do, in your own words?
What did the kidney mean by 'half of enough'?
Why did the doctors need to check Revathi's and Sudha's blood first?
What was different about the kidney's new home?
The kidney says, 'So this is what all that spare was for.' What was it for?

ideas.idea: You are a team of organs, and no organ works alone.
ideas.more: The heart pumps blood to the kidneys and the brain. The lungs put oxygen into the blood. The brain controls how fast the heart beats. The kidneys keep the blood clean for all of them. Draw these links on the organ map and they make a web.
One kidney, one lung or part of a liver can be enough. Spare capacity is why people can give organs, run long races and recover from illness.

ideas.idea: All human bodies share one plan, so parts can be shared.
ideas.more: A kidney from a sister, a cornea from a stranger, blood from a donor: they can work in another person because all human bodies are built the same way. Medicines help the new body accept them.

unknowns: Why do some people's kidneys fail with no known cause? In parts of Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Sri Lanka and Central America, many farm workers get kidney disease that is not explained by diabetes or high blood pressure. Heat, losing too much water, farm chemicals and drinking water have all been suggested. Nobody knows for sure.
How does the brain, made of 86 billion nerve cells, produce thoughts and feelings? Nobody knows.
Could we one day grow new organs from a person's own cells, so nobody waits for a donor? Scientists are trying, but no grown organ is in regular use yet.
